whyDescription: Most visitors to Portugal never come this far north. They stop at Porto, an hour south, or fly straight to the Algarve. The Minho is what they miss: a strip of country between the Minho river, which is the border with Spain, and the Douro, where the Atlantic meets granite mountains and everything in between is green. It rains here more than anywhere else in Portugal, and that is precisely the point — the vineyards climb every hillside, the rivers run all year, the forests of Peneda-Gerês are the country's only national park, and the beaches, long and cold and empty, belong to surfers and fishermen rather than sun loungers. This is also where Portugal was born: Guimarães was the first capital, Braga the oldest archdiocese, and the villages of the Lima and Cávado valleys have kept a way of life that the south lost decades ago. Portugal Active started here, in Viana do Castelo, and it is still where most of our homes are: manor houses in the Lima valley, beach lodges on the coast from Esposende to Caminha, and mountain retreats on the edge of the park. Everything is between twenty and sixty minutes from Porto airport, and nothing feels like it.
highlights: Vinho Verde — the world's only green wine region, with quintas open for tastings in the Lima and Cávado valleys
Peneda-Gerês National Park — granite peaks, wild horses, waterfalls and thermal springs, ninety minutes from the coast
Atlantic beaches from Esposende to Moledo — long, clean and empty, with surf, kitesurf and dunes
Viana do Castelo, Ponte de Lima and Guimarães — three of the most handsome historic towns in Portugal
The best seafood and the best festivals in the country — Agonia in August, harvest in September

seoDescription: Portugal's greenest region: Atlantic beaches, Vinho Verde quintas, the Peneda-Gerês mountains and historic towns. When to go, how to get there and our homes.
howToGetHere: Porto airport (OPO), 45 to 70 minutes by car depending on the valley. Vigo airport (VGO) in Spain is one hour from the coast. Direct trains from Porto to Viana do Castelo in about 75 minutes. We arrange airport transfers for every stay.
bestTimeToVisit: Late May to June and September to early October: warm and mostly dry, vineyards at their greenest or in full harvest, and beaches without crowds. July and August for the ocean and the festivals. Winter is mild, green and wet — the best rates of the year.
whatToExpect: A working, rural Atlantic region rather than a resort. Fishing boats at dawn, granite villages, vines trained on pergolas over every road, mountains an hour from the beach, and some of the best seafood in Portugal. Weather that changes by the hour and a pace of life that does not.
whereToStayIntro: Portugal Active was founded in Viana do Castelo and the Minho is still where most of our homes are — around fifty of them, from beach lodges with heated pools at Cabedelo and Carreço to restored manor houses in the Lima valley around Ponte de Lima, riverfront watermills at Caminha, and stone retreats on the edge of Peneda-Gerês. Every one is operated by the team that lives here.
journalSectionTitle: From the journal — stories from the Minho
thingsToDoIntro: The Minho rewards a base and a car. From any of our homes, the coast, the valleys and the mountains are each within an hour, so most guests spend a day on each. What follows is what our concierge team recommends to a first-time visitor with four or five days.

items.name: Praia do Cabedelo
items.description: Viana do Castelo's town beach, across the river from the centre: three kilometres of sand backed by dunes and pines, a Blue Flag every year, and Portugal's most consistent conditions for surf, windsurf and kitesurf. Ten minutes from the historic centre by car or ferry.

items.name: Moledo and Âncora
items.description: Twenty-five minutes north of Viana. Moledo is the Minho's most fashionable beach, sheltered by the Ínsua fort on its island; Vila Praia de Âncora, next door, has a fishing harbour and a river beach for children. The Lisbon set has summered here for a century.

items.name: Esposende and Ofir
items.description: Thirty minutes south. The Litoral Norte natural park: dunes, pine forest, the Cávado estuary and the Apúlia windmills. Quieter than Viana, better for long walks and cycling on the boardwalks.

items.name: Monte de Santa Luzia
items.description: The basilica above Viana do Castelo and, according to National Geographic, one of the finest panoramas in the world. Take the funicular from the station or drive up; the view runs from the Lima estuary to the Galician hills.

items.name: Ponte de Lima
items.description: Portugal's oldest town, chartered in 1125, on a bend of the Lima river with its medieval bridge, plane-tree avenue and the country's largest fortnightly market. Thirty minutes from Viana. The heart of Vinho Verde's Loureiro country and where several of our manor houses are.

items.name: Vinho Verde quintas
items.description: The region's producers — Quinta do Ameal, Aphros, Quinta de Soalheiro further up at Melgaço, and dozens of family estates — open for tastings by appointment. Loureiro and Alvarinho are the grapes to know; the harvest runs from mid-September into October.

items.name: Braga and Bom Jesus do Monte
items.description: Fifty minutes from the coast. Portugal's oldest city and religious capital, with a baroque staircase sanctuary that is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the country's finest sights at dusk.

items.name: Guimarães
items.description: One hour. The birthplace of Portugal, with a medieval centre listed by UNESCO and the castle where the first king was born. Combine it with Braga in a single day.

items.name: Peneda-Gerês National Park
items.description: Portugal's only national park, ninety minutes from Viana. Granite peaks, oak forest, wild Garrano horses, the Arado and Tahiti waterfalls, Roman milestones on the old Geira road and the thermal spa town of Gerês. Hike in the morning, swim in a river pool in the afternoon.

items.name: Soajo and Lindoso
items.description: Two mountain villages on the park's western edge, famous for their clusters of granite espigueiros — raised grain stores on stilts, some four hundred years old. Lindoso also has a castle and Portugal's largest group of espigueiros, seventy of them together.

items.name: Serra d'Arga
items.description: The wild sierra between Viana and Caminha: a plateau of granite, heather and river pools, with a monastery at its heart and views over the Atlantic. Our Hike, Dive and Dine experience is here — a morning walk, a swim in a natural pool and lunch in a village restaurant.

seasons.spring: March through May. Highs climb from around sixteen to twenty-two degrees and the rain eases but never quite stops. The Atlantic is still cold, fourteen to fifteen degrees, and best left to surfers. What spring offers is the Minho at its most spectacular: vineyards in early leaf, camellias in every garden, waterfalls in Gerês at full strength, and rates well below summer. Easter is the exception — the processions in Braga fill the region's hotels.
seasons.summer: June through August. Warm and mostly dry, with highs of twenty-five to twenty-nine degrees and the coast cooled by the northerly nortada wind in the afternoons. The ocean stays cool, seventeen to nineteen degrees, swimmable for the hardy and ideal for surf and kitesurf. The river beaches of the Lima and the pools of Gerês are the local answer to the heat. August holds the region's largest festivals — Agonia in Viana in the third week — and is the one month to book months ahead.
seasons.autumn: September through November. September is the best month of the year: still summer-warm, the sea at its warmest, the crowds gone and the vindima — the grape harvest — filling the valleys from mid-month into October. Vineyards turn from green to copper. By late October the rain returns; November is wet, mild and quiet, with chestnut fairs and the first Alvarinho of the new vintage.
seasons.winter: December through February. Mild by northern European standards, with highs around fourteen to fifteen degrees, but the wettest months of the year — the reason everything is so green. The Atlantic is cold and the surf serious. Viana's Christmas lights, wood fires in the manor houses, a heated pool under grey skies and the lowest rates of the year. Gerês occasionally sees snow on the high ground.
seasons.bestForFirstTime: Late May to June, or September. Both give warm, mostly dry weather of twenty to twenty-six degrees, the vineyards at their greenest or at full harvest, empty beaches and easy restaurant tables. June is better for the ocean and long days; September is better for atmosphere — the harvest, the warm sea, the slower pace before the rain returns.

transport.byAir: Porto's Francisco Sá Carneiro airport is the arrival point for the whole region: forty-five minutes to Viana do Castelo, fifty to Ponte de Lima, thirty-five to Esposende and roughly an hour and a half to the Gerês villages, all by motorway. Vigo airport in Spanish Galicia is one hour from Caminha and Viana and worth considering for travellers connecting through Madrid. Lisbon is three and a half to four hours by motorway.
transport.byTrain: Comboios de Portugal runs the Linha do Minho from Porto Campanhã to Viana do Castelo in about seventy-five minutes and on to Caminha and Valença; Braga and Guimarães have direct urban trains from Porto in around an hour. There is no railway into the Lima valley or the mountains — for those, a car or our transfers.
transport.byCar: The A28 motorway runs up the coast from Porto to Viana and Caminha and is toll-free through the Viana section; the A3 runs inland to Braga, Ponte de Lima and the Spanish border at Valença. Driving here is easy, distances short, and a car is the only practical way to combine coast, valley and mountains in one stay. Foreign-plated cars should register for the electronic tolls before arrival.
transport.fromSpain: From Galicia, the A3 crosses at Valença-Tui: one hour from Vigo to Viana, under two from Santiago de Compostela. Most of our Spanish guests drive; the Minho river is the border, and the towns on both banks — Valença and Tui, Monção and Salvaterra — are a day out in themselves.
transport.gettingAround: A car is essential outside the towns. Viana, Ponte de Lima, Braga and Guimarães are all compact and walkable once you arrive. The Ecovia do Lima cycle path follows the river for seventy kilometres from Viana into the valley — the best way to reach a quinta without driving. Our concierge arranges transfers, drivers and bicycles for every home.

eatDrinkIntro: The Minho eats better than anywhere in Portugal and knows it. This is the country of caldo verde, of rojões and sarrabulho, of lampreia in late winter and sardines in June, of bacalhau baked with broa and of the freshest Atlantic seafood served in tasquinhas owned by the fishermen's families. Wine is Vinho Verde — light, dry, slightly sparkling and, in its Alvarinho and Loureiro forms, among the best white wines in Europe. Below, the places our team sends guests.

restaurants.name: Tasquinha da Linda
restaurants.description: Viana do Castelo. Owned by fish wholesalers; the freshest seafood on the coast, on the harbour. Reservation essential.

restaurants.name: Camelo
restaurants.description: Santa Marta de Portuzelo, Viana do Castelo. Regional Portuguese cooking at Rua de Santa Marta, 119.

restaurants.name: O Marinheiro
restaurants.description: Vila Praia de Âncora. Grilled fish metres from the harbour it came from. Simple, loud and exactly right.

restaurants.name: Mercado Municipal de Viana
restaurants.description: Weekday mornings. The fish hall is one of the best in the country; buy for the house and let our chef cook it.

specialties.name: Bacalhau à moda de Viana
specialties.description: Salted cod baked with peppers, onions, potatoes and broa cornbread — the coast's signature plate.

specialties.name: Rojões and sarrabulho
specialties.description: Marinated pork with a rice cooked in pig's blood; the winter Sunday lunch of the Lima valley.

specialties.name: Vinho Verde
specialties.description: Light, dry and faintly sparkling. Alvarinho from Monção and Melgaço and Loureiro from the Lima valley are the two to seek out.

specialties.name: Lampreia
specialties.description: River lamprey, cooked in its own blood with rice, from January to April — a delicacy the Minho takes very seriously.

experiencesIntro: The Minho is where Portugal Active began as an adventure company, and most of our own experiences still happen here, run by our own guides and partners we work with every week.

experiences.name: Horseback riding in Viana do Castelo
experiences.description: Beach, mountain and flower fields in a single morning from a stable ten minutes from the city.

experiences.name: Canyoning in Peneda-Gerês
experiences.description: Abseiling waterfalls, natural slides and pools in the national park, with our own guides. From age twelve.

experiences.name: SUP descent of the Lima river
experiences.description: A gentle paddle downstream from Ponte de Lima between vineyards and Roman bridges.

experiences.name: Hike, Dive and Dine in Serra d'Arga
experiences.description: A morning walk on the sierra, a swim in a granite river pool and lunch in a village restaurant.

experiences.name: Vinho Verde tasting in the Lima valley
experiences.description: A morning at a working quinta with the producer — four to six wines, regional cheese and bread.

experiences.name: Surf lessons on the Minho coast
experiences.description: Cabedelo's consistent beach break, with a school that has taught here for twenty years.

eventsIntro: The Minho's calendar is the most festive in Portugal. The two dates that matter for planning are both in August, in Viana do Castelo; the harvest in September is the quieter reward.

events.name: Romaria de Nossa Senhora d'Agonia
events.description: Portugal's most famous romaria, held since 1772: gold-filigree costume parades, flower carpets, boat processions and fireworks over the Lima. Homes on the coast book out months ahead.

events.name: Neopop
events.dates: August · next dates to be announced
events.description: One of Europe's most respected electronic music festivals, on the old fortress by the sea.

events.name: Feiras Novas
events.description: The Lima valley's great fair, held since 1826: markets, folk groups, a giant Sunday procession and the best gigantones in the north.

events.name: Vindima
events.description: The Vinho Verde harvest. Quintas take visitors into the vines and the wineries; the valleys smell of must for a month.

events.description: The most important Easter processions in Portugal, in the country's religious capital.

events.name: Festa de São João
events.description: Midsummer night: bonfires, grilled sardines, plastic hammers and fireworks in every town.

faqs.question: How many days do I need in the Minho?
faqs.answer: Four to five days is the comfortable length: a day on the coast, a day in the Lima valley with a quinta visit, a day for Braga and Guimarães, and a day in Peneda-Gerês. A week lets you slow down and add the mountain villages and the Alvarinho country around Monção and Melgaço.

faqs.question: Is the Minho good for a beach holiday?
faqs.answer: Yes, for Atlantic beaches and surf. Sea conditions and water temperature vary with the season. For a stay with a heated pool, use the search filter and check the selected home’s heating conditions and any additional charge.

faqs.question: Do I need a car?
faqs.answer: Yes, unless you are staying in Viana do Castelo itself and happy to use trains and our transfers. The region's appeal is the combination of coast, valley and mountains, each within an hour, and only a car makes that easy.

faqs.question: How far is the Minho from Porto?
faqs.answer: Forty-five to seventy minutes by motorway from Porto airport, depending on the home. Viana do Castelo is seventy-five minutes from Porto by direct train.

faqs.question: When is the Vinho Verde harvest?
faqs.answer: From mid-September into October, depending on the year and the grape. Loureiro in the Lima valley is picked first; Alvarinho in Monção and Melgaço a little later.

faqs.question: Is Peneda-Gerês a day trip from the coast?
faqs.answer: Yes — ninety minutes each way. For canyoning, the waterfalls and the villages of Soajo and Lindoso, leave early. If the mountains are the point of the trip, several of our homes are on the park's edge.

faqs.question: What is the weather like?
faqs.answer: Atlantic: mild all year, warm and mostly dry from June to September, wet and green from November to March. Pack a layer even in summer.

faqs.question: Is the Minho suitable for families?
faqs.answer: Very. River beaches with warm, calm water, farm animals at the quintas, gentle bike paths along the Lima, and homes with gardens and pools. Our concierge organises babysitters and family-friendly experiences.

name: Viana do Castelo
tagline: Northern Portugal's Atlantic capital, where the Lima meets the ocean.
description: A complete guide to Viana do Castelo, the third most welcoming city in the world.
heroSubtitle: Northern Portugal's Atlantic capital, where the Lima meets the ocean

pullQuote.text: The beaches of Viana do Castelo are some of the most beautiful in the country.

primaryAccolade.text: Third most welcoming city in the world
primaryAccolade.note: First Portuguese city ranked in the global top three

whyDescription:
Few visitors travel this far north. Most stop at Porto, ninety minutes south, or detour for the Algarve. Those who continue along the coast find a working Atlantic city built on cod fishing and Eiffel-trained engineering, with seventeenth-century townhouses leaning over granite squares and, in late August, one of the largest traditional festivals in Portugal.

Viana do Castelo sits where the Rio Lima reaches the Atlantic, about seventy-five kilometres north of Porto. The municipality counts roughly eighty-six thousand residents and runs from the open ocean to the wooded edges of the Peneda mountains. It received its royal charter from King Afonso III on 18 June 1258 and became a city in 1848. For most of its history it looked outward, to the sea: shipyards on the river, codfishing fleets running the long voyage to the banks of Newfoundland, sugar trade with the Brazilian northeast, and an ironwork tradition that produced the gold-filigree jewellery still worn at the city's main festival.

The civic heart is the Praça da República, a Renaissance square that has held the same function for more than five hundred years. The fountain at its centre dates to 1554. The fortress-like former town hall and the loggia of the Casa das Varandas, built in 1589 for the Misericórdia brotherhood, stand on opposite sides. The granite is dark, the proportions human, the scale closer to a Tuscan hill town than to anything else in Portugal.

Above the city, on the Monte de Santa Luzia, a neo-Byzantine sanctuary commands the Lima estuary from two hundred and fifty metres. Designed by the architect Miguel Ventura Terra and built between 1904 and 1943, the basilica is reached by Portugal's longest funicular — six hundred and fifty metres of track, inaugurated in 1923 — or by a path of one hundred and sixty-eight steps. The view from its esplanade, of the river meeting the ocean and the town laid out below, was described by National Geographic Magazine in 1927 as rivalled in the world only by those of Rio de Janeiro and Funchal.

The waterfront has been worked, not curated. The Gil Eannes, a 1955 hospital ship built in the local shipyards to support the cod fleet on the Newfoundland and Greenland banks, is moored on the riverfront as a museum. The Ponte Eiffel, drawn in Gustave Eiffel's Paris office and inaugurated on 30 June 1878, was the first two-level iron bridge over the Lima and remains in daily use, carrying both road and rail. The Centro Cultural, designed by the Pritzker laureate Eduardo Souto de Moura, sits a short walk upriver, part of a small ensemble that also includes work by Fernando Távora and Álvaro Siza.

The setting works in seasons. The Atlantic stays cool, between sixteen and eighteen degrees in summer, which makes Praia do Cabedelo — a one-kilometre crescent of fine sand reached by a five-minute river ferry — one of the leading windsurf and kitesurf beaches in Portugal. Praia Norte, in the city itself, holds Blue Flag status and two saltwater tidal pools, one shallow enough for children. Inland, the Lima valley runs east through one of the original sub-regions of the Vinho Verde appellation, the birthplace of the Loureiro grape, with manor estates around Ponte de Lima opening for tastings.

The town is at its most itself in the third week of August, during the Romaria de Nossa Senhora d'Agonia. The festival has been held since 1772. Boats are decorated and taken in procession to the sea. Women appear in the gold-filigree costume of the Alto Minho, which the local jewellers' tradition still produces. Fireworks are launched over the Lima. The accommodation books out months in advance.

What the rest of the year offers is quieter. Tap-water espresso at granite cafés. Friday market under the bridge. A funicular climb at dusk. Cod fritters at a marble counter. A drive twenty minutes inland to find a quinta that has been making white wine from Loureiro vines for four generations.

Most travellers who come to Northern Portugal stop short of Viana. The ones who continue find that the city has stayed on its own scale, more Atlantic than Mediterranean, and that its accolade — third most welcoming city in the world, ranked by Booking.com in 2024 from more than three hundred million verified reviews — was earned by the same restraint that keeps it interesting.

thingsToDoIntro: What follows is what locals would recommend to a first-time visitor with three days. The historic centre is small enough to walk in an afternoon. The hilltop deserves its own morning. The waterfront is a separate world, between river and ocean. And what lies outside the city — the Lima valley, Ponte de Lima, Caminha at the Spanish border, Peneda-Gerês — is the reason most return visitors come back for a second stay.

seasons.spring: March through May. Highs climb from roughly eighteen to twenty-one degrees; rain eases but remains a feature of the calendar. The Atlantic is still cold, around fourteen degrees, and best left to surfers. What spring offers instead is the Minho at its greenest: vineyards in early leaf, camellias and wildflowers along the river, low crowds, and rates well below summer.
seasons.summer: June through August. Warm and dry, with August highs reaching twenty-six degrees and only twenty-nine to thirty-eight millimetres of rain across the month. The ocean stays cool at sixteen to eighteen degrees, swimmable for the hardy and ideal for surf, windsurf, and kitesurf at Cabedelo. Early August holds the city's two largest events — Neopop in the first week and the Romaria d'Agonia in the third — which together make this the tightest accommodation window of the year.
seasons.autumn: September through November. September stays summer-warm, around twenty-five degrees, before a sharp cooling and the return of significant rain by October. The Lima valley vindima, or grape harvest, runs from September into early October, and the vineyards turn from green to copper. Early autumn is one of the best windows in the year. By November, it is genuinely wet.
seasons.winter: December through February. Mild by European standards, with highs around fifteen degrees, but the wettest and darkest months: between one hundred and eighty and two hundred and thirteen millimetres of rain per month. The Atlantic is cold and the surf serious. The historic centre is lit for Christmas — thirty-six illuminated locations and a market that runs from early December to early January — and rates are at their lowest of the year.
seasons.bestForFirstTime: Late May to June and September. The combination is consistent across all three months: warm, drier weather with highs of twenty to twenty-five degrees, vineyards either at their greenest or at full harvest, and crowds that are manageable rather than absent. June is best for beach time and long days; September is best for atmosphere — the harvest, the slower pace, the warmth holding before the rain returns.

transport.byAir: Porto's Francisco Sá Carneiro airport, sixty-five to seventy kilometres south, is the default arrival point — forty-five to fifty minutes by car on the A28, which became toll-free through the Viana section in January 2025. Vigo airport in Spanish Galicia, about seventy-eight kilometres north, is a sensible alternative for travellers connecting via Madrid or already in Spain. Lisbon is four hours by motorway and only justified if you are starting your trip in the capital.
transport.byTrain: Comboios de Portugal runs direct services on the Linha do Minho from Porto Campanhã. Faster trains cover the route in one hour and fifteen to twenty-five minutes, with departures roughly hourly at peak. Fares range from eight to sixteen euros one-way. Viana station sits eight hundred metres from the historic centre — a ten-minute walk, or two minutes by taxi.
transport.byCar: From Porto, the A28 covers the seventy kilometres in forty-five to fifty minutes and is largely toll-free near Viana, with only the Angeiras and Póvoa gantries closer to Porto still active. The coastal N13 is slower and more scenic, threading through fishing villages and beach towns. Drivers in vehicles with foreign plates should register for Easytoll or Via Verde before crossing the border to avoid manual toll collection.
transport.fromSpain: The most direct route from Galicia is the A3 motorway, crossing into Portugal at Valença-Tui — one hour from Vigo, one hour and forty-five minutes from Santiago de Compostela. ALSA and FlixBus run buses on the same axis with a transfer at Valença. The Caminha-A Guarda ferry has been suspended since 2020, with a 2026 reopening discussed but not confirmed; the Xacobeo Transfer water taxi currently substitutes for pilgrims walking the Caminho Português da Costa.
transport.gettingAround: The historic centre is compact and walkable. The Ecovia do Lima cycle path follows the riverbank for seventy kilometres, the most direct way into the Vinho Verde valley by bicycle. Parking in the centre is metered; the main municipal car park is at Campo d'Agonia, with roughly one thousand and sixty spaces, near the waterfront. Uber operates but thinly compared to Porto or Lisbon. A car is unnecessary for the city itself, useful for the valley and the coast.

eatDrinkIntro: Viana does not have the Michelin density of Porto or Lisbon, but it has what those cities have largely lost: working-day restaurants run by the same families for three or four generations, fish that arrived that morning, and a generation of younger chefs returning to take regional cooking somewhere new. Two restaurants in the city hold Michelin Bib Gourmand status. The Pousada de Santa Luzia, on the hilltop, has the view. Below the bridge, on the river, the wholesalers sell to the restaurants in the morning and feed visitors in the evening.

restaurants.name: Tasquinha da Linda
restaurants.description: Owned by fish wholesalers. The freshest seafood in town. Reservation essential.

restaurants.name: Camelo
restaurants.description: Santa Marta de Portuzelo, Viana do Castelo. Regional Portuguese cooking at Rua de Santa Marta, 119.

restaurants.name: Os 3 Potes
restaurants.description: Sixteenth-century tavern serving regional classics — arroz de polvo, bacalhau à Viana, leitão à Bairrada.

restaurants.name: A Laranjeira
restaurants.description: Family-run, no menu. Whatever came in on the boat that morning, cooked the way the owner's grandmother taught her.

restaurants.name: Pousada de Santa Luzia
restaurants.description: Hilltop dining at the basilica, with the same panorama National Geographic put in the same league as Rio de Janeiro. Reservations essential at sunset.

restaurants.name: Zé Natário
restaurants.description: Classic granite-counter pastelaria — cod fritters, bola de Berlim, milk-fed cinnamon coffees taken standing.

specialties.name: Bacalhau à moda de Viana
specialties.description: Salted cod baked with peppers, onions, potatoes and broa — the city's signature plate, on most menus year-round.

specialties.name: Arroz de polvo
specialties.description: Slow-cooked octopus rice; the Alto Minho version is wetter than the south's.

specialties.name: Lampreia do Lima
specialties.description: River lamprey, in season from January through April. A dish that polarises — those who love it return for it.

specialties.name: Vinho Verde Loureiro
specialties.description: The Lima valley is the Loureiro grape's place of origin. Crisp, low-alcohol, citric — drunk young and cold.

experiencesIntro: What follows is a selection of experiences that the concierge organizes, alone or in combination, for guests staying in Portugal Active homes. Each can be arranged with twenty-four hours' notice, most with less. None requires a car: the concierge handles transfers, reservations, and (where relevant) the introductions to growers, winemakers, and instructors who do not generally accept walk-ins.

experiences.name: Vinho Verde tasting in the Lima valley
experiences.description: A morning at a working quinta in the Loureiro grape's place of origin — typically four to six wines tasted with the producer, paired with regional cheese and bread. Twenty to thirty minutes from the city by car.

experiences.name: Atlantic surf or windsurf at Cabedelo
experiences.description: Private or small-group lessons at one of Portugal's leading windsurf and kitesurf beaches. Wetsuits and equipment included. Suitable for beginners through advanced; conditions best from late spring through early autumn.

experiences.name: Kayaking the Lima estuary
experiences.description: From the marina upriver toward the wooded banks above the Eiffel bridge, with a stop at a small beach for swimming when conditions allow. Guided by a local instructor.

experiences.name: Day trip to Caminha and the Spanish border
experiences.description: Twenty-one kilometres north to a smaller riverside town on the Minho estuary, with a walled medieval-Renaissance core, a fountain from the same stoneworker as Viana's, and a view across to Galicia. Combined easily with a lunch stop on the way back.

experiences.name: Peneda-Gerês National Park
experiences.description: Portugal's only national park, an hour by car inland: granite villages, mountain trails, and the long-haired Garrano horses that have lived in these mountains since the Roman period. Best done as a guided private day.

experiences.name: Funicular ride to Santa Luzia at golden hour
experiences.description: The classical evening: the six-and-a-half-minute climb to the sanctuary, the panorama of the river meeting the ocean, dinner at the Pousada restaurant with the same view. Reservations are essential.

eventsIntro: Two events dominate Viana's calendar, both in August, both worth planning either toward or around. Several smaller events through the year offer reasons to visit out of season — the spring blues festival on the Praça, the autumn vindima, the Christmas illuminations in the historic centre. Accommodation in Viana follows the festival calendar more sharply than elsewhere in the Norte.

events.name: Romaria de Nossa Senhora d'Agonia
events.description: The city's flagship festival, held annually since 1772. Boat processions, gold-filigree costume parades, fireworks over the Lima. Accommodation books out months in advance.

events.name: Neopop Electronic Music Festival
events.dates: August · next dates to be announced
events.description: International electronic music on the waterfront. The first week of August is the tightest accommodation window of the year together with the Romaria.

events.name: Wine & Blues Festival
events.description: Vinho Verde producers and blues acts on the Praça da República. The unofficial start of the spring travel season.

events.name: Vindima do Vinho Verde
events.description: Grape harvest across the Lima valley. Many quintas open their doors for working-harvest visits.

events.name: Christmas illuminations
events.description: Thirty-six illuminated locations in the historic centre, with an artisan market under the Eiffel bridge.

events.name: Carnaval
events.description: Smaller and more traditional than Torres Vedras or Madeira, but characteristically Minho — masked figures, regional brass bands, sardines on the grill.

pressIntro: The city has been written about consistently but not heavily — which is part of its appeal. The selection below is drawn from English-language travel coverage of the past decade and from the Booking.com global ranking that placed Viana, in 2024, as the third most welcoming city in the world.

faqs.question: How many days do I need in Viana do Castelo?
faqs.answer: Two to three days suit most first-time visitors: one for the historic centre and the Santa Luzia hilltop, one for the beaches and waterfront, and a third for day trips into the Lima valley or to Ponte de Lima. As a base for the wider Alto Minho — including Peneda-Gerês and the Vinho Verde quintas — four to five days is the comfortable length.

faqs.question: What is the best time to visit Viana do Castelo?
faqs.answer: Late May or September. The Atlantic is at its warmest, the city is full but not crowded, and the restaurant calendar runs at full strength. Mid-August coincides with the Romaria d'Agonia — book a year ahead if you want to be here for it.

faqs.question: Is Viana do Castelo worth visiting from Porto?
faqs.answer: Yes — and it is a different experience. Porto is a busy compact city; Viana is a working coastal town with empty beaches, granite squares and a slower rhythm. The train takes 75 minutes, so day-trips are easy, but two nights does the city justice.

faqs.question: What is Viana do Castelo famous for?
faqs.answer: Three things. The Basílica de Santa Luzia on the hill above the city. The Romaria de Nossa Senhora d'Agonia, one of Portugal's most important religious festivals. And the cod-fishing fleet — the Gil Eannes hospital ship moored on the Lima river is a working museum to that history.

faqs.question: How do I get from Porto to Viana do Castelo?
faqs.answer: Comboios de Portugal runs an intercity train from Porto Campanhã to Viana in 75 minutes for €8.90 one way. By car, the A28 motorway takes one hour. The scenic alternative — the N13 coast road — adds 30 minutes.

faqs.question: Where are the best beaches in Viana do Castelo?
faqs.answer: Praia Norte for families (calm, breezy, lifeguarded). Cabedelo across the river for surfers and walkers (five kilometres of empty sand). Praia do Afife, twenty minutes north, for the wildest stretch.

faqs.question: What language is spoken in Viana do Castelo?
faqs.answer: Portuguese. English is widely spoken in restaurants, hotels and shops in the historic centre. Spanish is understood by most adults; French by older generations.

faqs.question: Is Viana do Castelo safe for families?
faqs.answer: Yes — among the safest small cities in Europe. Praia Norte is lifeguarded in summer. The historic centre is walkable, well-lit and pedestrianised. Healthcare is excellent (Hospital de Santa Luzia is five minutes from any of our properties).

faqs.question: What is the typical food in Viana do Castelo?
faqs.answer: Bacalhau à moda de Viana (salted cod, baked with peppers and onions). Arroz de polvo (octopus rice). Lampreia in season (river lamprey, January–April). Sardines on the grill all summer. Vinho Verde — always cold, always young.

faqs.question: How far is Viana do Castelo from the airport?
faqs.answer: Porto airport (OPO) is 70 kilometres south — one hour by car on the A28 motorway. We arrange private transfers from OPO to any of our Viana properties.

faqs.question: What are the best villas to rent in Viana do Castelo?
faqs.answer: We operate twelve properties in and around Viana — from restored stone farmhouses in the Lima valley to contemporary villas above the Cabedelo dunes. All include daily housekeeping, local concierge and private chef on call. See our Viana collection above.

name: Caminha
tagline: A walled border town at the mouth of the Minho, facing Galicia across the estuary.
description: A guide to Caminha: the walled town at the mouth of the Minho, Moledo beach, the Camarido pines and the Coura valley.
heroSubtitle: Where the Minho meets the Atlantic, with Galicia on the far bank
whyDescription:
Caminha is the last Portuguese town on the Atlantic coast before Spain. It sits on the south bank of the Minho estuary, a few kilometres before the river reaches the ocean, and looks straight across the water at Galicia and the wooded cone of Monte de Santa Tecla. For most of its history that view was a frontier. Today it is a ten-minute boat ride.

The old town is small and still defined by its walls. The oldest sections date from the thirteenth century, and the Torre do Relógio, the clock tower on the main square, was the principal gate through them. In front of it, on the square locals call the Terreiro, stands a granite fountain built between 1551 and 1553 by the master mason João Lopes o Velho, who also made the fountain in Viana do Castelo's Praça da República. The Solar dos Pitas, a Gothic townhouse, and the old town hall share the square. A short walk along the Rua Direita leads to the Igreja Matriz, a granite parish church begun around 1488 and built over some sixty years, with Manueline carving at the chancel and a carved wooden Mudéjar ceiling inside.

The coast begins just beyond the town. The Mata Nacional do Camarido, a pine forest planted on the sands at the river mouth, runs down to the estuary beach of Camarido, where the Galician shore feels close enough to touch. South of it is Praia de Moledo, a long open beach of fine sand facing the island of Ínsua, where a seventeenth-century fort encloses the remains of a Franciscan convent. Moledo has been the summer beach of northern Portuguese families for generations. It is broad, clean and often windy, which keeps it cool in August and makes it a good beach for kitesurfing and long walks.

Inland, the town opens onto two valleys. Upstream along the Minho, the road passes Seixas and Lanhelas on the way to Vila Nova de Cerveira and the fortress town of Valença. To the south and east, the River Coura runs down from the hills through a green valley of maize fields, granite villages and old watermills. At Vilar de Mouros an old stone bridge crosses the river beside a village whose name has been attached, since 1971, to one of the most celebrated editions of any Portuguese music festival. Behind it all rises the Serra d'Arga, a granite massif where Garrano horses graze freely.

The crossing to Spain is part of daily life. The car ferry that linked Caminha with A Guarda for decades stopped in 2020, defeated in the end by the sandbanks of the estuary. Small licensed water taxis now make the crossing in about ten minutes, carrying mostly pilgrims on the coastal route of the Camino de Santiago, which passes through the town. By road, the bridges at Vila Nova de Cerveira and Valença put Galicia fifteen to twenty-five minutes away.

The rhythm is seasonal. In late winter and spring the Minho brings lamprey and shad to local tables. In summer Moledo fills, the river beaches of the Coura warm up, and the music festivals of the valley arrive in August. Outside those weeks the town returns to its own scale: a coffee on the Terreiro, a walk under the pines to watch the tide turn at the river mouth, dinner as the lights come on across the water in Galicia.

Praia de Moledo and the Camarido pine forest at the mouth of the Minho
Water taxis across the estuary to A Guarda in Galicia
The Coura valley, Vilar de Mouros and the Serra d'Arga
Lamprey and shad from the Minho in late winter and spring

howToGetHere: Porto airport (OPO) about 1h by the A28. Vigo airport (Spain) about 50 min. Viana do Castelo 25 min south. Regional trains on the Linha do Minho stop at Caminha and Moledo.
bestTimeToVisit: June and September. Long days, a warm Coura for river swimming and Moledo without the August crowds. Late winter and spring for the lamprey season.
whatToExpect: A small walled town on a wide estuary, with pine forest, an Atlantic beach and Galicia on the other bank. Quiet most of the year, lively in August.
whereToStayIntro: Most of our homes in Caminha are at a three-hundred-year-old granite watermill on the River Coura in Vilar de Mouros, ten minutes inland from the town. The mill and the stone houses around it are let as separate homes, from a one-bedroom loft to a four-bedroom house, or together as one estate for up to twenty guests, with the river beach at the foot of the garden. On the coast, a beachfront house at Moledo has three suites and a pool that faces the sunset. All of them are looked after by our team in the Alto Minho, the same team that runs our homes in Viana do Castelo, twenty-five minutes south.
journalSectionTitle: From the journal: stories from Caminha
thingsToDoIntro: Caminha is small enough to see on foot in a morning, and most of its interest lies in what surrounds it: the river mouth, the beach, the Coura valley and the Galician shore. What follows is how we would spend three days here.

items.name: Torre do Relógio
items.description: The clock tower was the main gate of the medieval walls, whose oldest sections date from the thirteenth century. Walk through it from the square into the Rua Direita, the old main street.

items.name: Chafariz do Terreiro
items.description: Granite fountain built between 1551 and 1553 by João Lopes o Velho, the mason behind Viana do Castelo's fountain. A national monument since 1910.

items.name: Igreja Matriz
items.description: Parish church begun around 1488 and built over some sixty years. Manueline carving at the chancel and a carved Mudéjar ceiling in wood.

items.name: Praça Conselheiro Silva Torres
items.description: The square locals call the Terreiro, with the fountain, the Gothic Solar dos Pitas, the old town hall and café tables. The centre of the town's social life.

thingsToDo.heading: The river mouth and the coast

items.name: Mata Nacional do Camarido
items.description: Pine forest planted on the dunes between the town and the sea, with shaded trails that end at the estuary beach of Camarido, facing Galicia.

items.name: Praia de Moledo
items.description: A long Atlantic beach of fine sand facing the island of Ínsua. Wide, clean and often windy, which suits walkers, kitesurfers and anyone escaping the heat.

items.name: Ínsua
items.description: A small rocky island off Moledo, with a seventeenth-century fort built around an older Franciscan convent. Best seen from the beach.

items.name: Vila Praia de Âncora
items.description: Fishing harbour and beach town ten minutes south, with the small Fortim da Lagarteira and, just inland, the Neolithic Dólmen da Barrosa.

items.name: Vilar de Mouros and the Coura
items.description: Granite village on the River Coura, ten minutes from the town, with an old stone bridge, river beaches and the festival that has carried its name since the 1970s.

items.name: Serra d'Arga
items.description: Granite mountain behind Caminha, with free-roaming Garrano horses, small villages and the monastery of São João de Arga. Best walked in spring and autumn.

items.name: Vila Nova de Cerveira
items.description: Riverside town fifteen minutes upstream, home since 1978 of one of Portugal's longest-running art biennials, with a bridge across to Galicia.

items.name: Valença
items.description: Star-shaped fortress town facing Tui across the Minho, twenty-five minutes upstream. Walk the ramparts, then cross the old iron bridge on foot to Tui cathedral.

items.name: A Guarda and Monte de Santa Tecla
items.description: Galicia, on the far bank. A water taxi from Caminha takes about ten minutes. Above A Guarda, the Iron Age settlement on Monte de Santa Tecla looks back over the whole estuary.

seasons.spring: March to May. The valleys are at their greenest and the Coura runs full. Highs climb from around seventeen to twenty-one degrees, and rain is still a regular visitor. The lamprey and shad season on the Minho runs through these months, and the trails of the Serra d'Arga are at their best. The sea is cold, around fourteen degrees.
seasons.summer: June to August. Warm and mostly dry, with highs in the mid-twenties and a northerly wind, the nortada, that blows most afternoons on the coast and keeps Moledo cool. The ocean stays at sixteen to eighteen degrees; the river beaches of the Coura are warmer. August is the busiest month, with the festivals of Paredes de Coura and Vilar de Mouros and full beaches.
seasons.autumn: September to November. September is often the best month of the year: warm days, a quiet beach and the grape harvest in the valleys. October brings the first heavy rain and turning leaves along the Coura. By November the town is back to its winter rhythm.
seasons.winter: December to February. Mild but wet, with highs around thirteen to fifteen degrees and regular Atlantic storms. The estuary is at its most dramatic and the town at its quietest. The lamprey season opens around the turn of the year.
seasons.bestForFirstTime: June or September. Both give warm, settled weather and the full range of the place, from beach and river swimming to walks in the Serra d'Arga, without the crowds and accommodation pressure of August.

transport.byAir: Porto's Francisco Sá Carneiro airport is about ninety-five kilometres south, roughly an hour by car on the A28. Vigo airport in Galicia is around fifty minutes by road, via the bridges at Valença or Vila Nova de Cerveira, and a sensible alternative for connections through Madrid. We arrange private transfers from either.
transport.byTrain: Regional trains on the Linha do Minho, which runs from Porto to Valença, stop at Caminha, Moledo and Vila Praia de Âncora. From Porto Campanhã allow around two hours, sometimes with a change at Viana do Castelo. Caminha station is a short walk from the old town.
transport.byCar: The A28 runs from Porto along the coast to Caminha, passing Viana do Castelo twenty-five kilometres to the south. The N13 coast road is slower and follows the beaches and fishing towns. Drivers of cars with foreign plates should register with an electronic toll service before arriving, as several motorways near Porto use electronic gantries.
transport.fromSpain: From Vigo or Santiago de Compostela, cross the Minho by the motorway bridge at Tui and Valença, or by the bridge between Goián and Vila Nova de Cerveira, then follow the river road down to Caminha. On foot or by bicycle, water taxis cross from A Guarda in about ten minutes, weather and tides permitting.
transport.gettingAround: The old town is compact and best on foot. The Camarido forest and Moledo can be reached on foot or by bicycle, and much of the Minho riverbank upstream towards Vila Nova de Cerveira has a cycle and walking path. For the Coura valley, the Serra d'Arga and the beaches further south, a car makes life easier.

eatDrinkIntro: Caminha eats from the river and the sea. In late winter and spring the Minho brings lamprey and shad, cooked in ways that have barely changed in a century, and restaurants across the valley plan their year around the season. The fishing harbour at Vila Praia de Âncora, ten minutes south, supplies the grilled fish that fills summer menus along the coast. The wine is Vinho Verde, and upstream in Monção and Melgaço it is made from Alvarinho, the grape behind the region's finest whites. Our concierge keeps a short list of tables, from family tascas in the old town to riverside restaurants in the Coura valley, and books them for guests.

specialties.name: Grilled fish from Âncora

experiences.description: A guided paddle from the town towards the river mouth, between the Camarido pines and the Galician shore, with a stop on a sandbank when the tide allows.

experiences.description: A water taxi across the estuary, then up to the Iron Age settlement above A Guarda for the view back over Caminha and the river mouth. Lunch in the Galician fishing port before returning.

experiences.description: A guided day on the granite mountain behind the town, through small villages and upland pasture where Garrano horses graze, with a stop at the monastery of São João de Arga.

experiences.description: A morning upstream with an Alvarinho producer, tasting the region's finest white wines, followed by lunch in the valley.

experiences.description: Lessons for beginners and improvers on the long beach at Moledo, where the summer afternoon wind suits kitesurfing. Equipment included.

experiences.name: Cycling the Minho riverbank
experiences.description: An easy ride upstream on the riverside path towards Vila Nova de Cerveira, with Galicia across the water all the way. Bicycles arranged by the concierge.

eventsIntro: Caminha's calendar is set by the river and by August. The lamprey season fills restaurants from winter into spring; the music festivals of the Coura valley fill the region in the second half of August, when homes should be booked well ahead.

events.name: Paredes de Coura Festival
events.description: One of Portugal's best-known alternative music festivals, held since 1993 in a natural amphitheatre beside the Taboão river beach, about forty minutes from Caminha.

events.name: Vilar de Mouros Festival
events.dates: Late August, dates announced each year
events.description: Rock festival on the banks of the Coura, ten minutes from Caminha. Its 1971 edition made it a landmark in Portuguese music history.

events.name: Lamprey season
events.description: Restaurants in Caminha and along the Minho build their menus around the river's lamprey, and later its shad.

faqs.question: How many days do I need in Caminha?
faqs.answer: Two days cover the town, the Camarido forest and Moledo. With four or five you can add the Coura valley, the Serra d'Arga, a crossing to A Guarda and a day upstream in Valença or the Alvarinho country of Monção and Melgaço.

faqs.question: Is there still a ferry from Caminha to A Guarda?
faqs.answer: The car ferry stopped in 2020 and is not running. Small licensed water taxis cross the estuary to A Guarda in about ten minutes, weather and tides permitting, and are used mainly by pilgrims on the Camino. By car, the nearest bridges are at Vila Nova de Cerveira and Valença.

faqs.question: What is the best beach near Caminha?
faqs.answer: Praia de Moledo, a long Atlantic beach just south of the town, facing the island of Ínsua. For calmer water, the estuary beach at Camarido faces Galicia across the river mouth. In summer, the river beaches of the Coura are warmer than the ocean.

faqs.question: When is the best time to visit Caminha?
faqs.answer: June and September for weather and space. August for the festivals and the busiest beaches. Late winter and spring for the lamprey season and the valleys at their greenest.

faqs.question: How far is Caminha from Porto?
faqs.answer: About ninety-five kilometres, roughly an hour by car on the A28 from Porto airport. Regional trains from Porto take around two hours.

faqs.question: Is Caminha a good base for visiting Galicia?
faqs.answer: Yes. A Guarda is across the estuary, Tui is about twenty-five minutes away by road, Vigo under an hour, and Santiago de Compostela under two hours.

faqs.question: What is Caminha known for?
faqs.answer: Its walled old town and clock tower, its position on the Minho facing Spain, Moledo beach and the river's lamprey. It is also a stage on the coastal route of the Portuguese Camino de Santiago.

faqs.question: Is Caminha good for families?
faqs.answer: Yes. The town is small and walkable, Moledo is lifeguarded in the bathing season, and the river beaches of the Coura offer calmer water for younger children. Our watermill homes, which can be booked together, suit groups of several generations.

name: Esposende
tagline: Where the Cávado meets the Atlantic, between protected dunes and pine forest.
description: A guide to Esposende: the Litoral Norte natural park, Ofir and Apúlia, the Cávado estuary and the dunes, forty minutes north of Porto.
heroSubtitle: Protected dunes, pine forest and the Cávado estuary, forty minutes north of Porto
whyDescription:
Esposende is the stretch of the northern coast that most people drive past. The A28 runs a few kilometres inland, and from the motorway there is little to suggest what lies between the road and the sea: sixteen kilometres of beach, dune and pine forest, protected as a natural park, with a small town at the mouth of the Cávado river in the middle of it.

The Parque Natural do Litoral Norte covers the whole coastline of the municipality, from the mouth of the Neiva in the north to the southern edge of Apúlia. It was first protected in 1987 and became a natural park in 2005, and most of its area lies at sea, over reefs and rocky seabed. On land it protects a fragile system of dunes, pine woods and salt marsh of a kind that has largely disappeared elsewhere on this coast. Wooden walkways cross the dunes, and a coastal cycle path links the beaches.

The town sits on the north bank of the Cávado, where the river widens into an estuary sheltered by a long sand spit. The Forte de São João Baptista, built between 1699 and 1704 to guard the river mouth, still stands on the waterfront, with a red iron lighthouse on its southwest corner. An iron bridge from 1892 crosses the river to Fão, a riverside village known across the north for its clarinhas, a small fried pastry filled with squash jam and egg. Beyond Fão lies Ofir, a pine forest on the dunes with a long beach at the end of it and, offshore, the dark rocks known as the Cavalos de Fão.

Further south is Apúlia, the village that gave this coast its best-known trade. For generations the people of Apúlia gathered sargaço, the seaweed brought in by the Atlantic, dried it on the sand and sold it as fertiliser to the farms inland. The sargaceiros worked in the surf in a white woollen tunic called the branqueta, and the stone windmills on the dunes above the beach, built to grind grain, are still the landmark of the village. The harvest is no longer an economy, but it lives on through the village's folk group and in local memory.

Behind the coast the land rises gently towards Barcelos and Braga. On a hill above Vila Chã, the Castro de São Lourenço preserves the foundations of an Iron Age settlement, with a view down the whole shoreline. Braga, with its cathedral and the sanctuary of Bom Jesus do Monte, is thirty minutes away. Viana do Castelo is twenty-five minutes north, and Porto forty minutes south.

Esposende is a beach town in summer and a quiet one the rest of the year. The northerly wind that blows most summer afternoons keeps the beaches cool and brings windsurfers and kitesurfers to the coast. Families come back year after year for reasons that have not changed much: long beaches with room to spare, fish on the grill, and a pace that suits them.

howToGetHere: Porto airport (OPO) about 35 min by the A28. Braga 30 min east. Viana do Castelo 25 min north. No railway: the nearest stations are Barcelos and Viana do Castelo.
bestTimeToVisit: June and September. Warm days, long beaches with space to spare, and the afternoon wind that suits windsurf and kitesurf. July and August for full summer.
whatToExpect: A low-key beach town on a river mouth, inside a coastal natural park. Dunes, pines and wide beaches rather than cliffs and nightlife.
whereToStayIntro: Our homes in Esposende are two apartments by the sea, both suited to families and small groups. One is a three-bedroom apartment in Marinhas with a balcony, five hundred metres from the beach and the natural park. The other is a sea-view duplex on the Avenida dos Banhos, the seafront avenue, with three bedrooms over two floors. Both are a short walk from the beach and the town, and both are looked after by our team in the Minho. Guests who want a house with a pool often combine the coast here with our homes around Viana do Castelo, twenty-five minutes north.
journalSectionTitle: From the journal: stories from Esposende
thingsToDoIntro: Esposende is a place for long walks and slow days rather than sightseeing lists. The coast is the reason to come, and it changes from north to south: river mouth and town, pine forest and dune, then the old seaweed-harvesting village of Apúlia. What follows is how we would divide it.

items.name: Forte de São João Baptista
items.description: Built between 1699 and 1704 to defend the mouth of the Cávado, with the red iron lighthouse of Esposende on its southwest corner.

items.name: Cávado estuary
items.description: The river widens into a sheltered estuary behind a long sand spit. Calm water for paddleboard and kayak, and salt marsh for wading birds.

items.name: Ponte de Fão
items.description: Iron bridge from 1892 across the Cávado, linking the Esposende side of the river with the village of Fão.

items.name: Fão
items.description: Small riverside village on the south bank, known across the north of Portugal for the clarinhas de Fão pastry.

items.name: Ofir
items.description: A long beach at the end of a pine forest on the south bank of the river, with the offshore rocks known as the Cavalos de Fão.

items.name: Dune walkways
items.description: Wooden walkways cross the protected dunes of the natural park, so you can walk for kilometres behind the beach without damaging the plants that hold the sand.

items.name: Apúlia
items.description: Beach village at the southern end of the park, with its row of stone windmills on the dunes and the memory of the sargaceiros, the seaweed harvesters.

items.name: The northern beaches
items.description: North of the town, towards the Neiva river, the beaches get wilder and quieter, backed by dunes and farmland.

items.name: Castro de São Lourenço
items.description: Iron Age hill settlement above Vila Chã, with the foundations of stone houses and a view along the whole coast.

items.name: Barcelos
items.description: Twenty minutes inland, home of the Barcelos cockerel and one of the largest weekly markets in Portugal, held on Thursdays.

items.name: Braga
items.description: Thirty minutes east. The cathedral, the old centre and the sanctuary of Bom Jesus do Monte, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2019, with its baroque stairway and water-powered funicular.

items.name: Viana do Castelo
items.description: Twenty-five minutes north: the basilica of Santa Luzia, the historic centre and more Atlantic beaches.

seasons.spring: March to May. The dunes flower and the pine woods smell of resin. Highs rise from about seventeen to twenty-one degrees, with showers still frequent. The sea is cold, but the walkways and the coastal cycle path are at their best, and the beaches are empty.
seasons.summer: June to August. Warm and mostly dry, with highs in the mid-twenties. The nortada, a steady northerly wind, blows most afternoons, keeping the beaches cool and bringing windsurfers and kitesurfers. The water stays at sixteen to eighteen degrees. July and August are the family months, busiest in the first half of August.
seasons.autumn: September to November. September is warm and quiet, often the best month for the beach. October brings the first heavy rain and the Atlantic swell. By November the coast belongs to fishermen and walkers again.
seasons.winter: December to February. Mild, wet and windy, with highs around fourteen degrees. Atlantic storms make for dramatic walks along the dunes. Many beach restaurants close or shorten their hours, and the town settles into local life.
seasons.bestForFirstTime: June or September. Warm enough for the beach, quiet enough to have long stretches of it to yourself, and with the best light for walking the dunes and the estuary.

transport.byAir: Porto's Francisco Sá Carneiro airport is about forty kilometres south, around thirty-five minutes by car on the A28. It is the natural arrival point, and we arrange private transfers to our homes. Vigo airport in Galicia is about an hour and a quarter north.
transport.byTrain: Esposende has no railway station. The nearest are Barcelos, on the Linha do Minho about twenty minutes inland, and Viana do Castelo, twenty-five minutes north; from either, a taxi covers the rest. Buses also run between Porto and Esposende.
transport.byCar: From Porto, the A28 reaches Esposende in about forty minutes. The A11 links the town to Barcelos and Braga. The N13, the old coast road, runs through the town and is the slower, more local way to Viana do Castelo. Drivers of cars with foreign plates should register with an electronic toll service before arriving.
transport.fromSpain: From Vigo, cross the Minho at Tui and Valença and follow the motorways south by way of Ponte de Lima and Viana do Castelo, about an hour and a quarter in all. From Santiago de Compostela allow around two hours.
transport.gettingAround: The town, the beach and the estuary are all walkable, and a coastal cycle path follows much of the natural park. A car is useful for Braga, Barcelos and Viana do Castelo, less so for day-to-day life by the sea.

eatDrinkIntro: Esposende's table is the coast's table: Atlantic fish grilled over charcoal, seafood rice for sharing, and in Fão a pastry tradition worth the detour. The restaurants along the seafront at Apúlia and beside the Cávado work to the season and the catch, and most of them are small and family-run. The wine is Vinho Verde from the Cávado, one of the sub-regions of the appellation. Our concierge keeps a short list of tables along the coast and books them for guests.

specialties.name: Clarinhas de Fão
specialties.description: A half-moon of thin fried pastry filled with doce de chila, a squash jam, and egg yolk, then rolled in sugar. Made in Fão and sold in its pastry shops.

specialties.name: Grilled fish
specialties.description: Sea bass, bream and, in summer, sardines, grilled over charcoal and served with boiled potatoes, greens and olive oil.

specialties.name: Arroz de marisco
specialties.description: Seafood rice, loose and brothy in the northern style, brought to the table in the pot and meant for sharing.

specialties.name: Vinho Verde from the Cávado
specialties.description: One of the sub-regions of the Vinho Verde appellation, known for fresh, citric whites. Drunk young and cold, with fish.

experiencesIntro: What follows are experiences our concierge arranges for guests staying in our Esposende homes. Most need a day's notice, and the concierge can arrange transfers wherever a car would otherwise be needed.

experiences.name: Paddleboard or kayak on the Cávado estuary
experiences.description: A guided session on the sheltered water behind the sand spit, with the fort and lighthouse on one side and the pines of Ofir on the other.

experiences.name: Windsurf or kitesurf lessons
experiences.description: Lessons for beginners and improvers on a coast where the afternoon northerly blows reliably through the summer. Equipment included.

experiences.name: Walking the dunes of the natural park
experiences.description: A guided walk with a local naturalist along the walkways and through the pine woods, explaining how the dune system works and why it is protected.

experiences.name: Braga and Bom Jesus
experiences.description: A day in Braga: the cathedral, the old centre and the baroque stairway of Bom Jesus do Monte, coming back down on the water-powered funicular.

experiences.name: Barcelos market
experiences.description: Thursday morning at one of the largest weekly markets in Portugal, for pottery, produce and the painted cockerels.

experiences.name: Vinho Verde tasting
experiences.description: A visit to a Vinho Verde producer inland, with a tasting of the region's whites and lunch among the vines.

faqs.question: How far is Esposende from Porto?
faqs.answer: About forty kilometres. Porto airport is around thirty-five minutes by car on the A28, and the centre of Porto around forty-five.

faqs.question: What are the best beaches in Esposende?
faqs.answer: Ofir, at the end of a pine forest on the south bank of the Cávado, and Apúlia, with its windmills, are the best known. The town beach is within walking distance of the centre, and the beaches to the north, towards the Neiva river, are the quietest.

faqs.question: What is the Parque Natural do Litoral Norte?
faqs.answer: A natural park covering the sixteen-kilometre coastline of Esposende, from the Neiva river to Apúlia. It protects dunes, pine forest, salt marsh and a large marine area. It was first protected in 1987 and became a natural park in 2005.

faqs.question: Is Esposende good for families?
faqs.answer: Yes. The beaches are long and uncrowded, the estuary offers calmer water, and the town is small and easy to get around. The main beaches are lifeguarded in the bathing season. Both of our apartments by the sea suit families.

faqs.question: Who were the sargaceiros of Apúlia?
faqs.answer: The seaweed harvesters of Apúlia, who gathered the sargaço brought in by the Atlantic, dried it on the sand and sold it as fertiliser to farms inland. They worked in a white woollen tunic called the branqueta, and the tradition is kept alive by a local folk group.

faqs.question: When is the best time to visit Esposende?
faqs.answer: June and September for warm weather without crowds. July and August for full summer, when the town is at its liveliest. Spring and autumn suit walkers and cyclists.

faqs.question: Is Esposende a good base for Braga, Porto and Viana do Castelo?
faqs.answer: Yes. Braga is thirty minutes east, Barcelos twenty, Viana do Castelo twenty-five minutes north and Porto forty minutes south, which makes Esposende a practical coastal base for the north of Portugal.

whyDescription:
The city that gave Portugal its name. Port wine cellars lining the riverbank. Michelin starred restaurants in converted warehouses. A creative energy that makes Lisbon feel mainstream. Porto is compact, walkable, and endlessly rewarding for those who take the time to explore beyond the postcard views.

Beyond the city, the Douro Valley unfolds in terraced vineyards classified as a UNESCO World Heritage landscape. This is where port wine comes from, but it is also where Portugal's most exciting table wines are being made. Visit a quinta, taste with the winemaker, and understand why this region is considered one of Europe's most beautiful.

name: Douro Valley
tagline: Terraced vineyards above the river, in one of the oldest regulated wine regions in the world.
description: A guide to the Douro Valley: the UNESCO Alto Douro wine landscape, the quintas, Pinhão, Régua and Lamego, the railway and the harvest.
heroSubtitle: Terraced vineyards, schist and a river that shaped a wine region

pullQuote.text: Wine has been produced by traditional landholders in the Alto Douro region for some 2,000 years.

primaryAccolade.note: Demarcated in 1756, one of the oldest regulated wine regions in the world

whyDescription:
The Douro is a wine region built by hand. Over some two thousand years, and above all in the last three centuries, the people of the valley cut terraces into steep slopes of schist, held them up with dry-stone walls and planted vines where almost nothing else would grow. The result is one of the most recognisable landscapes in Europe, and one of the few wine regions where the landscape itself is the reason to come.

The region was demarcated in 1756, when the Marquis of Pombal created a company to regulate the production and trade of port, which makes it one of the oldest regulated wine regions in the world. In 2001 UNESCO inscribed the Alto Douro Wine Region, about twenty-four thousand hectares at the heart of the demarcated area, as a World Heritage cultural landscape. The valley is traditionally divided into three parts: the Baixo Corgo around Régua, greener and wetter; the Cima Corgo around Pinhão, the heart of port production; and the Douro Superior, hotter and wilder, running east to the Spanish border.

For most of its history the river was the only road out. Port travelled down to the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia in flat-bottomed rabelo boats until the railway and then the road took over, and in the twentieth century a chain of dams turned the rapids into a series of calm reaches. Today the Douro is navigable from Porto to the Spanish border, and river boats pass through locks such as the one at Carrapatelo, which lifts them about thirty-five metres. The Linha do Douro railway follows the water for much of its way from Régua to Pocinho, and at Pinhão the station walls carry twenty-four azulejo panels from 1937 showing the harvest, the boats and the landscape.

Pinhão, a small town where the Pinhão river joins the Douro, is the centre of the Cima Corgo, surrounded by some of the best-known quintas in port. Peso da Régua, downstream, is the region's commercial town and home of the Museu do Douro. South of the river, Lamego climbs to the baroque sanctuary of Nossa Senhora dos Remédios, reached by a stairway of 686 steps. The viewpoints are part of the experience: Casal de Loivos above Pinhão, São Leonardo de Galafura above Régua, and São Salvador do Mundo near São João da Pesqueira.

Most visitors come for a day from Porto and see the valley from a boat or a coach. Staying changes it. The quintas open their doors for tastings, the light on the terraces shifts from hour to hour, and the evenings are quiet in a way that day visitors never see. The valley is at its most alive at harvest, from late August into October, when grapes are still picked by hand on the steepest slopes and, at some quintas, trodden by foot in granite lagares.

It is also a place of extremes. Summers in the Cima Corgo are among the hottest in Portugal, and winters are cold, with morning fog filling the valley. Spring, with the vines in new leaf, and autumn, with the terraces turning red and gold, are the seasons locals would choose.

seoTitle: Douro Valley: Quintas, Wine and Where to Stay | Portugal Active
seoDescription: Terraced vineyards, port quintas and river towns in the UNESCO Alto Douro. What to see in the Douro Valley, when to go, and where to stay.
